title: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)
hookLine: each tribal leader brings an identical gift, and each is listed in full

cards: At a graduation, the dean reads every single name. Three hundred students, and each one walks across the stage, shakes the same hand, takes the same rolled-up paper. It takes forever.
Somebody in the back row checks their phone. Wouldn't it be faster to say congratulations, everyone? Sure.
But ask any parent in the audience whether it's the same. Numbers chapter seven makes the slow choice on purpose, twelve times in a row, and the chapter grows long because of it.

teach.b: The Tabernacle is finished and anointed, and the leaders of the twelve tribes come forward to dedicate the altar. Each leader is called a nasi, from the same root as naso: one who is lifted up.
They bring their gifts one per day, for twelve days.

teach.h: EACH ONE WRITTEN OUT IN FULL.
teach.b: On the first day, Nachshon, of Judah: one silver dish and one silver basin, both full of fine flour mixed with oil; one golden pan full of incense; a bull, a ram, a lamb, a goat, and more for the peace offerings.
On the second day, the leader of Issachar brings exactly the same. And the third. Down to the shekel.
And the Torah writes it out every time: twelve paragraphs, almost word for word, then a grand total. Eighty-nine verses. An editor might cut it.
The commentators asked why it stays. Nachmanides answers that God wanted to honor each leader equally.
Each chose to bring the gift on his own day, and the Torah wouldn't let anyone be summarized as the same as the one before.
A midrash goes further: the gifts were identical, but each leader had his own meaning in mind, tied to his own tribe's story.
This chapter is also read in synagogue during Hanukkah, because its theme is dedication. The Hebrew for dedication of the altar is chanukat hamizbe'ach. Hanukkah is the same word.

how: Numbers 7, the gifts of the tribal leaders, is read in synagogue as part of Naso and again, a day at a time, during the eight days of Hanukkah, the festival of dedication.

games.q: you're the scribe. twelve leaders have brought identical gifts. how do you record them?

write all twelve out in full, then the total.

practice: Think of a good thing lots of people around you do so often it blurs: the parents who all pack lunches, the nurses on the night shift, the volunteers who show up every Sunday.
Pick out one of them and give them their own paragraph in your mind: their name, their face, the way they do it. Then another, without summarizing.
